questions.stem: The SI unit of work is the
questions.explanation: Work is force multiplied by distance, so its unit is the newton metre, which is given the special name joule. One joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves a body 1 m along its line of action.

distractorRationale.a: The newton measures force alone, without the distance factor
distractorRationale.b: The watt measures power, which is work per unit time
distractorRationale.d: The pascal measures pressure, which is force per unit area

questions.stem: A porter walks 100 m along a level road carrying a heavy load on his head at constant speed. The work done by him on the load is

options.text: zero, because the supporting force is perpendicular to the motion
equal to the weight of the load multiplied by 100 m
equal to the mass of the load multiplied by 100 m
negative, because the load resists being carried

questions.explanation: The force supporting the load acts vertically upwards while the displacement is horizontal, so the angle between them is 90°. Since $W = Fs\cos 90^{\circ}$ and $\cos 90^{\circ} = 0$, the work done on the load is zero even though the porter certainly feels tired.

distractorRationale.b: Multiplies the vertical force by a horizontal distance, ignoring that only the component along the motion counts
distractorRationale.c: Multiplies a mass by a distance, which does not even give the units of work
distractorRationale.d: Negative work needs a force opposing the motion; the supporting force is at right angles to it

questions.stem: A horizontal force of 50 N pushes a box 8.0 m across a floor in the direction of the force. Calculate the work done. Give your answer in joules.
questions.explanation: The force and displacement are in the same direction, so $\cos\theta = 1$ and $W = Fs = 50 \times 8.0 = 400\ \text{J}$.

questions.stem: Calculate the kinetic energy of a car of mass 1000 kg moving at 20 m/s. Give your answer in joules.
questions.explanation: $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(1000)(20)^2 = \frac{1}{2}(1000)(400) = 200\,000\ \text{J}$, that is $2.0 \times 10^5\ \text{J}$ or 200 kJ. Square the velocity before multiplying — using 20 instead of 400 would give only 10 000 J.

questions.stem: A bucket of mass 5.0 kg is lifted vertically through a height of 4.0 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the gain in its gravitational potential energy. Give your answer in joules.
questions.explanation: $E_p = mgh = 5.0 \times 10 \times 4.0 = 200\ \text{J}$. The gain in potential energy equals the minimum work that must be done against gravity to raise the bucket.

questions.stem: A body of mass 2.0 kg falls freely from rest through a height of 20 m. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, its speed on reaching the ground is
questions.explanation: By conservation of mechanical energy, $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh$, and the mass cancels to give $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 20} = \sqrt{400} = 20\ \text{m/s}$. The 2.0 kg is deliberately redundant information.

distractorRationale.d: Used 2gh = 400 as the speed itself instead of taking its square root

questions.stem: A rope inclined at 60° to the horizontal is used to drag a crate 10 m along level ground. If the tension in the rope is 100 N, the work done is
questions.explanation: Only the horizontal component of the tension does work: $W = Fs\cos\theta = 100 \times 10 \times \cos 60^{\circ} = 100 \times 10 \times 0.5 = 500\ \text{J}$.

distractorRationale.b: Used sin 60° = 0.866 instead of cos 60°, which resolves the force the wrong way
distractorRationale.c: Ignored the angle entirely and used W = Fs
distractorRationale.d: Multiplied by the angle in degrees rather than by its cosine

questions.stem: If the speed of a moving vehicle is doubled while its mass stays the same, its kinetic energy becomes
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$, so it is proportional to the square of the speed. Replacing $v$ by $2v$ gives $\frac{1}{2}m(2v)^2 = 4 \times \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. This is why stopping distances grow so sharply with speed.

distractorRationale.a: Kinetic energy depends directly on speed, so it cannot stay the same
distractorRationale.b: This would be true if kinetic energy were proportional to v, but the v is squared
distractorRationale.d: Cubing rather than squaring the factor; that would apply if energy went as v³

questions.stem: A ball of mass 0.50 kg is thrown vertically upwards with a kinetic energy of 100 J. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, calculate the maximum height it reaches. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: At the highest point all the kinetic energy has become potential energy, so $mgh = 100\ \text{J}$. Substituting, $0.50 \times 10 \times h = 100$, giving $5h = 100$ and $h = 20\ \text{m}$. You could check via the launch speed: $\frac{1}{2}(0.50)v^2 = 100$ gives $v = 20\ \text{m/s}$, and $\frac{v^2}{2g} = \frac{400}{20} = 20\ \text{m}$.

questions.stem: A pendulum bob of mass 0.20 kg is displaced until it is 0.45 m above its lowest point and then released. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, calculate its speed as it passes through the lowest point. Give your answer in metres per second.
questions.explanation: Potential energy at release $= mgh = 0.20 \times 10 \times 0.45 = 0.90\ \text{J}$. All of this becomes kinetic energy at the lowest point, so $\frac{1}{2}(0.20)v^2 = 0.90$, giving $v^2 = 9.0$ and $v = 3.0\ \text{m/s}$. The mass cancels, so $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ gives the same result directly.
